abstract: High temperatures reprogram gene regulatory responses and are particularly deleterious for crop yield, especially when these events occur at night. This emphasizes that partitioning of heat responses is based on time of day. Coordination between time of day and environmental responses relies on the circadian clock. However, the precise regulatory mechanism of how the clock achieves this partitioning at different levels of gene regulation is poorly understood. Using circadian clock mutants with altered CCA1 and LHY expression, we generated a time-resolved transcriptome, proteome, and metabolome following a short-term heat stress in Arabidopsis. We identified regulatory connections specific to CCA1 and LHY, as well as those shared with other clock components linked to heat stress responses. Additionally, new connections between CCA1 and LHY and non-cycling genes highlight a broader role for the clock in regulating heat responsive gene expression. CCA1 and LHY regulated processes, such as sulfur assimilation and ROS scavenging, may contribute to time-of-day specific thermotolerance. Overall, heat responses were dampened in both the transcriptome and proteome in cca1lhy, suggesting both transcriptional and post-translational circadian-regulated processes are important for heat responses. Lastly, we identified differences in metabolic responses in cca1lhy and suggest a role for circadian regulation of starch degradation in thermotolerance. This study generates and utilizes data across levels of gene regulation to identify heat responses in the transcriptome and proteome regulated by CCA1 and LHY. These findings establish shared and distinct regulatory mechanisms of clock components in response to heat stress and provide new candidates for network integration and a foundation to engineer plants more tolerant to high temperatures depending on time of day.
